concepts.label: Overfitting means fitting the training data well while failing on unseen data; the training-vs-validation/test gap is the diagnostic
Detect overfitting by monitoring training vs validation loss/accuracy on held-out data; the divergence point marks its onset
Overfitting arises from excess model capacity relative to the training data: the model fits noise / memorizes instead of learning generalizable features

Regularization is the family of techniques that prevent overfitting by constraining the model; the canonical members are L1/L2 (weight decay), dropout, early stopping, data augmentation, and label smoothing
L2 regularization (weight decay) adds a squared-weight penalty to the loss, shrinking weights toward zero and yielding smoother decision boundaries that generalize better
In adaptive optimizers, L2 must be implemented as decoupled weight decay (AdamW), applying the decay directly to the weights rather than through the gradient; prefer AdamW over Adam + weight_decay

L1 regularization penalizes absolute weight values and drives exact zeros (sparsity, feature selection), unlike L2 which shrinks but rarely zeroes; L1 is consequently less used in deep learning than L2
Biases (and normalization parameters) are excluded from the L2/weight-decay penalty
Typical weight-decay values and their tuning context (moderate defaults; stronger for AdamW than SGD-CNN training)
Dropout mechanism: during training randomly set a fraction p of neurons/activations to zero; at test time use the full network
Inverted dropout: survivors are scaled by 1/(1-p) during training so that expected outputs are preserved and no test-time adjustment is needed
Never apply dropout at inference; forgetting model.eval() before evaluation is a common silent bug — always switch modes explicitly
Why dropout works: it prevents neuron co-adaptation and behaves as ensemble/model averaging over sub-networks
Standard dropout rates: strongest (~0.5) on large fully connected / hidden layers, weaker elsewhere; modern practice uses little or no dropout because other regularizers suffice
Dropout/regularizer placement: never on the output layer; concentrate where parameter count and overfitting risk are highest (the large FC layers)
Early stopping: halt training when validation loss stops improving (patience-based), and keep the checkpoint from the best-validation epoch
Label smoothing: replace one-hot targets with soft targets (smoothing ~0.1) to prevent overconfidence
Batch normalization has a regularization side effect: the noise of mini-batch statistics acts like dropout-style noise and improves generalization (though weaker than dropout)
Too much regularization causes underfitting: watch training loss and regularize less if it cannot decrease
Regularization deliberately trades training performance for generalization: a regularized model can be better despite lower training accuracy
Data augmentation: artificially expand the training set with label-preserving transformations; the practical remedy when data is limited, especially for vision
The standard vision-augmentation inventory: flips, crops, rotation, color jitter (plus mixup/cutmix as advanced image techniques)
Averaging multiple models (ensembling/bagging) yields more accurate, more robust predictions than any single model
Complementary framings of the overfitting phenomenon: master-ai's bias-variance decomposition apparatus vs the course's memorization/train-gap framing

Complementary evaluation-data hygiene rules: master-ai's leakage discipline (tune on validation, evaluate once on test) vs the course's deterministic-transforms rule (never augment validation/test data)
LayerNorm (not BatchNorm) is the standard normalization for Transformer/sequence architectures, because sequence lengths and batch statistics vary
